title: Salt in the river
hookLine: a lump of salt ruins a cup of water but is lost in the Ganges: a broad heart (AN 3, the salt crystal)

cards: Two people tell the same small lie on the same afternoon. One carries it for weeks, and it sours everything around it. The other notices, owns it, and by evening it has barely left a mark.

Same lie, same size, very different results. The Buddha takes up a sharper version of that puzzle, about karma. If every act brings back exactly what it deserves, measure for measure, how could anyone ever get free?
He answers with something from the kitchen.

teach.h: NOT EXACTLY AS YOU ACT, YOU REAP
teach.b: He begins by rejecting a claim.

If someone says that however a person acts, in exactly that way they'll experience the result, then, he says, there would be no living the holy life, no chance to make a complete end of suffering. Then the picture.
Suppose someone drops a lump of salt into a small cup of water.
Would the water become salty and undrinkable? Yes, sir, because the cup is small.
Now suppose they drop the same lump into the river Ganges. Would the river become undrinkable? No, sir, because the Ganges is a great mass of water.
The same small bad deed, he says, can lead one person to great suffering and barely touch another. The difference is in the person.
One is undeveloped in body, in conduct, in mind, in wisdom: limited, small-hearted, living with suffering. The other is developed, great-hearted, dwelling in the immeasurable.
For them the result of that small act is felt here and now, and not even a trace may appear beyond.

He adds a picture almost from a court: one person is jailed for stealing a tiny coin; another, rich and powerful, isn't jailed for the same amount. This isn't a teaching that small harms don't matter.
The salt is still salt. It's a teaching that the size of the heart changes what the salt does, and hearts can grow.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the salt simile to explain that karma is not a mechanical tit-for-tat, and many practitioners develop the immeasurables, kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, to widen the heart.

o: the river Ganges, sacred to many
salt, as in the lump lost in a river
a cup of water given to a guest

games.q: the salt crystal: tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha teaches that every act returns exactly measure for measure
he rejects that, saying it would leave no way to end suffering.
the salt simile says small harms don't matter
the salt is still salt; what changes is the heart it falls into.
the discourse also uses the picture of people jailed for a tiny theft
one is jailed for a tiny coin, another, powerful, is not.

games.q: someone asks you: if every act brings back exactly what it deserves, how can anyone get free? what does the Buddha answer?
o: a lump of salt ruins a cup but is lost in the Ganges.
small acts have no results at all.
games.why: the same small deed weighs differently depending on the heart it falls into, so freedom is possible.

practice: Recall one small thing that's been bothering you, a comment, a mistake, a slight, and feel how salty it tastes in a small cup.

Then let the cup widen: breathe into the chest and imagine the heart as wide as a river, with room for people you love, the sky, this whole day. Place that small salty thing into all of it, and notice whether the taste changes.

wordCard.voice: lona. The Pali word for salt, in the Book of Threes: a lump of salt ruins a small cup of water but is lost in the Ganges, since a small deed weighs differently in a broad, developed heart. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali lona: salt. the discourse is the Lonakapalla Sutta, the lump of salt.

carryVoice: Your line: widen your heart first. A practice of kindness and wisdom isn't only about avoiding new salt; it's about becoming a river. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.99 (Lonakapalla Sutta; AN 3.100 in some editions)
